title: This sea creature swims on a stack of jet engines, each one a cloned individual

cover.alt: A siphonophore colony seen against a grey background: a dark oval float on top of a column of transparent, cup-shaped swimming bells.

body: The siphonophore *Nanomia bijuga* looks like one animal, but it is a colony of clones. Its swimming bells, called **nectophores**, are jellyfish-like individuals that each squirt a jet of water, and new ones bud near the float at the top. The young, small bells up there do most of the steering, while the older, more powerful bells near the base supply most of the forward thrust. Working together, a colony may travel hundreds of metres up and down every day.

slides.alt: Black-and-white footage of a Nanomia bijuga colony swimming upward: a dark oval float leads a column of transparent swimming bells, with a tail of darker parts trailing below.
slides.caption: Filmed with a high-speed camera, a Nanomia bijuga colony swims up the frame: the dark float leads, and the stacked swimming bells beneath it pulse together.
slides.credit: Costello, Colin, Gemmell, Dabiri & Sutherland · CC BY 4.0 · excerpt

slides.heading: A division of labour among clones

left.label: Young bells, at the top
left.text: Smaller and weaker, but placed where a push twists the whole colony, so they do most of the turning.

right.label: Old bells, at the base
right.text: Bigger and stronger. Their backward jets provide most of the thrust that drives the colony forward.

slides.heading: A swimming stack about 2 cm long can travel 200 m a day
slides.note: The researchers' example colony: rising towards the surface at night, sinking by day

slides.heading: A marathon every day
slides.text: Scaled up to human size, the researchers say, that daily trip is like a 2 m tall person running a marathon every day. The colonies studied in the lab had between 4 and 12 swimming bells, each one a clone of the others.

slides.question: In a Nanomia colony, which swimming bells do most of the steering?
slides.explanation: The young bells are small, but sitting near the top lets them twist the colony. The older, bigger bells at the base mostly push it forward.

source.label: Costello et al. (2015), Nature Communications: Multi-jet propulsion in a colonial siphonophore
